US equity futures were mostly trending lower on Tuesday as traders await the latest financial results of some of Wall Street's largest banks.

The S&P 500 was down 0.2%, the Nasdaq 100 declined 0.5%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.6% in premarket trading. The Dow finished Monday trading higher for the third consecutive session, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite closed in the red.

Banking giants JPMorgan Chase (JPM), Goldman Sachs (GS), Wells Fargo (WFC) and Citigroup (C) are scheduled to report their third-quarter earnings before the bell. Bank of America (BAC) and Morgan Stanley (MS) are set to post their results on Wednesday.

Earlier in October, Oppenheimer said in a client note that earnings of certain major banks, including Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, are expected to be pressured amid broader concerns around capital markets revenue.

Treasury yields were down early Tuesday, with the two-year rate retreating 2.1 basis points to 4.77% and the 10-year rate off 0.5 basis points to 5.19%.

"With (third-quarter) earnings around the corner and the 10-year Treasury (greater than) 5.2% we think the debate around net interest income (NII) versus net interest margin (NIM) is becoming increasingly relevant for bank investors, and is largely centered in the regionals space," UBS Securities said in a note emailed on Monday.

UnitedHealth (UNH) shares rose 2.3% pre-bell as the health insurance giant raised its full-year earnings outlook. Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) decreased 1.1% as it reported its third-quarter results.

Domino's Pizza (DPZ) and Albertsons (ACI) are also expected to release their financials before the opening bell.

Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller, Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin and Boston Fed President Susan Collins are slated to speak on Tuesday.

The September existing home sales report is due at 10 am ET. Last month's consumer price index is due Wednesday, while September data on wholesale prices and retail sales post Thursday.

West Texas Intermediate crude oil and Brent each fell nearly 2% to $91.90 and $104.55 a barrel.

Stock futures were mixed Tuesday as several big banks and other notable companies reported quarterly results, with shares of memory chip makers falling for a second straight day on worries about Chinese competition.

Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 futures pointed 0.7% and fractionally higher, respectively, while Nasdaq 100 futures were 0.5% lower. Dow futures were aided by a rise in shares of UnitedHealth Group (UNH), which lifted its full-year profit guidance following a better-than-expected third quarter.

Yesterday, the tech-focused Nasdaq Composite and benchmark S&P 500 finished down a respective 0.4% and 0.1%, while the blue-chip Dow advanced 0.3%.

Earnings season kicks into high gear today with several big banks—JPMorgan Chase (JPM), Goldman Sachs (GS), Wells Fargo (WFC), and Citigroup (C)—and the likes of Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) reporting results before the bell.

Memory stocks headed lower for a second straight day after Chinese firm CXMT said over the weekend it plans on producing next-generation chips. Micron Technology (MU), Sandisk (SNDK), Seagate Technology (STX), and Western Digital (WDC) were down 2% to 4% premarket following Monday declines. Roundhill's Memory ETF (DRAM) was 3.5% lower after a nearly 4.5% pullback yesterday, and the broader iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) was headed a further 1% lower after falling 2.5% Monday.

Meta Platforms (META) stock slipped 0.5% before the bell following a nearly 3.5% rise. The Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF (MAGS), which tracks the group of seven mega-cap tech stocks, edged 0.3% lower after rising modestly yesterday.

After the U.S. bond market was closed yesterday in observance of Columbus Day, the 10-year Treasury yield pulled back four basis points from Friday's close to around 5.20%. Last Thursday, it briefly neared 5.37%, its highest level in more than 24 years.

Oil prices pulled back Tuesday, as investors weighed a diesel supply increase following President Donald Trump's controversial decision to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian energy against continued attacks on Saudi Arabia from Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen. U.S. benchmark West Texas Intermediate crude futures declined 2% to $91.85 a barrel, while front-month Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, fell 2% to around $104.50.

Bitcoin was trading around $83,400, up from overnight lows below $81,000. The U.S. dollar index, which tracks the value of the greenback against a basket of foreign currencies, declined 0.3% to 102.33. Gold futures rose 0.4% to $4,210 an ounce.

Investors' focus will turn to inflation readings the next two days, with the September Consumer Price Index reading tomorrow and the wholesale Producer Price Index on Thursday.

title: US Stock Futures Mixed as AI Concerns, LVMH Sales and Bank Earnings Shape Market Sentiment: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq, Wall Street

US Stock Futures Mixed as AI Concerns, LVMH Sales and Bank Earnings Shape Market Sentiment: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq, Wall Street
Fiona Craig

^DJI

US stock futures were mixed on Tuesday as investors assessed renewed concerns about artificial intelligence valuations, weaker-than-expected sales from luxury group LVMH and the approaching release of quarterly results from major Wall Street banks.

Geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and uncertainty surrounding oil supplies also remained important factors, while markets awaited US inflation data that could influence the Federal Reserve's interest rate decisions during the remainder of 2026.

Dow Jones Industrial Average futures rose 225 points, or 0.4%, by 02:48 ET (06:48 GMT), while S&P 500 futures slipped six points, or 0.1%. Nasdaq 100 futures declined 237 points, equivalent to 0.8%, reflecting continued pressure on technology shares.

The mixed performance followed an uneven session on Wall Street on Monday, when investors weighed concerns about the sustainability of artificial intelligence investment against rising energy prices and disappointing corporate updates.

Technology Shares Weaken Amid Questions Over AI Investment Returns

Technology stocks remained under pressure following losses among US semiconductor manufacturers at the beginning of the week.

An index tracking the semiconductor industry declined 2.7% on Monday, reflecting weaker sentiment towards companies exposed to artificial intelligence infrastructure spending.

The selling extended into Asian markets, where South Korean technology shares experienced substantial declines.

Reports of technological advances by Chinese memory chip manufacturer ChangXin Memory Technologies contributed to concerns about increasing competition between US and Chinese semiconductor companies.

Investors are assessing whether technological progress among Chinese manufacturers could narrow the competitive advantages held by established suppliers in the artificial intelligence market.

Concerns about the sector have also been influenced by questions surrounding revenue expectations at OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT.

Although demand for artificial intelligence technologies remains substantial, uncertainty persists over the financial returns that companies will generate from their investment programmes.

Major technology businesses are committing significant capital to data centres, semiconductor equipment and computing infrastructure, with some expenditure supported by borrowing.

The scale of these investments has increased scrutiny of future profitability and the ability of AI-related revenue growth to justify current valuations.

LVMH Shares Fall After Third-Quarter Sales Miss Expectations

Shares in luxury goods group LVMH (USOTC:LVMUY) declined in early Paris trading after the company reported third-quarter revenue below market expectations.

The group recorded revenue of €18.5 billion, representing organic growth of 1% compared with the same period a year earlier.

Analysts had expected organic growth of approximately 1.3%, according to Visible Alpha consensus estimates cited by Reuters.

The weaker-than-expected performance reflected continued difficulties in the Chinese luxury market, alongside softer demand for some of the group's principal fashion brands.

LVMH's fashion and leather goods division, which accounts for approximately half of total group revenue, recorded a 5% decline in organic sales.

That compared with analysts' expectations for a contraction of approximately 1.8%.

Growth in the group's watches and jewellery business also moderated during the quarter.

Across Asia, where China represents a major market for luxury products, revenue declined 5% year on year.

The downturn reflected weaker spending among Chinese consumers, with increased scrutiny of wealthy individuals' tax affairs adding to uncertainty in the luxury goods market.

Higher operating costs associated with geopolitical tensions have also presented challenges for luxury companies.

LVMH's results added to concerns about the pace of recovery in global demand for high-end products, particularly in China.

The figures may influence expectations for other European luxury goods manufacturers as investors assess consumer spending trends and the outlook for discretionary purchases.

Wall Street Banks Prepare to Report Third-Quarter Results

Investor attention was also turning towards the start of the US corporate earnings season, with several major financial institutions scheduled to release their third-quarter results on Tuesday.

JPMorgan Chase (NYSE:JPM), Goldman Sachs (NYSE:GS), Wells Fargo (NYSE:WFC) and Citigroup (NYSE:C) were among the banks expected to publish their latest financial statements.

The reporting calendar continues on Wednesday with results from Bank of America (NYSE:BAC), Morgan Stanley (NYSE:MS) and BlackRock (NYSE:BLK).

The figures will provide information about lending profitability, deposit costs, credit quality and activity in capital markets.

Investors will be particularly interested in how higher bond yields have affected banks' net interest margins and the valuations of their fixed-income portfolios.

Analysts at Vital Knowledge suggested that third-quarter results could broadly meet market expectations, although several risks remain.

The firm highlighted concerns about rising yields, weaker securities issuance and market volatility, which could affect investment banking fees and other capital markets revenue.

Income linked to residential mortgages could also face pressure.

Investment banking activity will be closely monitored for indications of whether corporate transactions, debt issuance and initial public offerings are recovering or remaining subdued.

In a separate assessment, Deutsche Bank analysts forecast third-quarter earnings growth of 34% for the broader S&P 500.

The bank suggested that consensus estimates may be too cautious, leaving room for companies to report results above expectations.

Corporate earnings will therefore be an important influence on market sentiment, particularly as investors assess whether profit growth can support current equity valuations.

Oil Prices Decline as Russian Supply Prospects Offset Middle East Risks

Oil prices moved lower on Tuesday following comments from Russia suggesting that diesel exports could exceed previously announced volumes under a supply arrangement with the United States.

Brent crude futures fell 1.5% to $105.09 per barrel by 03:54 ET, while West Texas Intermediate futures declined 1.8% to $92.08 per barrel.

Both contracts had risen during Monday's session, with Brent settling at its highest level since 15 September.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said late Monday that the country could restore diesel exports to levels above those outlined in the agreement announced by US President Donald Trump.

The comments followed Trump's announcement that his administration had temporarily eased sanctions affecting Russian fuel.

Trump also announced what he described as an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine.

However, uncertainty remained over the durability of the arrangement following reports of additional Russian strikes against Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

Meanwhile, developments in the Middle East continued to pose risks to international oil supplies.

Attacks attributed to Iran-backed Houthi forces on Saudi Arabia's international airport, alongside strikes targeting tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, contributed to concerns about the security of regional energy transport routes.

The Strait of Hormuz remains a strategically important passage for international oil shipments, making disruptions in the area particularly significant for global energy markets.

Although the prospect of additional Russian supply weighed on prices during Tuesday's session, geopolitical risks continued to influence expectations for crude oil availability.

The competing effects of potential supply increases and continuing Middle Eastern disruptions contributed to uncertainty in energy markets.

Looking ahead, investors will be monitoring the results of major US banks, forthcoming inflation figures, developments in the artificial intelligence sector and changes in global oil supply conditions.

Together, these factors will help determine market expectations for corporate profitability, interest rates and equity valuations during the remainder of the year.

Korean chipmakers plunge as CXMT raises competitive threat

South Korean memory-chip makers bore the brunt of the selloff. SK Hynix fell 8.9%, while Samsung Electronics dropped 8%. LG Innotek slid 8.9%.

The selloff followed reports that China's CXMT is advancing a higher-density 4F² DRAM design, with next-generation server-memory products targeted for year-end, raising competition concerns for established chipmakers. CXMT shares fell 2.4%.

Adding to pressure on South Korean equities, President Lee Jae Myung said the country would likely need to raise interest rates soon to narrow the gap with U.S. rates and align with global monetary tightening. South Korea's benchmark rate stands at 3.00%, below the Federal Reserve's 3.75%-4.00% range, raising the prospect of higher borrowing costs even as household debt and default risks remain concerns.

wall street stock market flag new york trading equity -Shutterstock

The benchmark US stock measures were mostly pointing higher before the opening bell Monday as traders await a busy week of corporate earnings and key inflation data.

The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.1% in premarket trading, while the Nasdaq 100 fell 0.1%. Equity markets finished Friday trading with weekly gains.

Wall Street banking giants JPMorgan Chase (JPM), Bank of America (BAC), Morgan Stanley (MS), Goldman Sachs (GS), Wells Fargo (WFC) and Citigroup (C) are expected to release their latest financial results this week, along with major corporations such as Johnson & Johnson (JNJ), UnitedHealth (UNH) and Charles Schwab (SCHW).

Investors also await the September consumer price index scheduled to be out on Wednesday, while data on wholesale prices and retail sales for the same month are due Thursday.

Treasury yields trended higher early Monday, with the two-year rate up 3.5 basis points to 4.79% and the 10-year rate up 0.9 basis points to 5.24%.

Last week, a preliminary survey of the University of Michigan showed that consumer sentiment fell to a five-month low in October as the one- and five-year inflation expectations reached their highest levels since May.

"Consumer sentiment dropped for the third consecutive month in October, with elevated gas prices and higher borrowing costs making consumers more worried about current economic conditions," Oxford Economics US Economist Grace Zwemmer said in remarks emailed to MT Newswires on Friday. "Both year-ahead and long-run inflation expectations ticked up, highlighting consumers' affordability concerns."

West Texas Intermediate crude oil inclined 0.9% to $92.67 a barrel, while Brent gained 0.8% to $105.64.

In a Truth Social post on Sunday, President Donald Trump announced Russia and Ukraine agreed to an energy ceasefire, with immediate effect. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia of violating the energy ceasefire after a strike on a power plant in Kharkiv, Reuters reported Monday.

Last week, Trump said on social media that Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to supply diesel to the US and global markets.

Trump also told reporters on Saturday that the US may join Saudi Arabia in its retaliation against Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels following an attack on Riyadh's international airport, according to CNBC. "We're going to look at it," Trump reportedly said. "We just found out about the recent attack. So, we'll make a decision."

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran is ready to provide assistance to help start dialogue between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi militants, according to Al Jazeera.

Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack is slated to speak at 12:50 pm ET.

Spot gold dipped 0.3% to $4,203 per troy ounce, while bitcoin decreased 0.2% to $83,435.
